map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Microloans are small loans for people whom banks turn away. People once hoped these loans would lift families out of poverty by helping them start businesses. Careful studies have cooled that hope. Most borrowers did not earn more, and their businesses rarely grew past a very small size. But the studies agree on a quieter benefit. The loans helped families with the timing of their spending. Families could get through lean months and pay for big, one-time costs they could not have managed otherwise. Microloans, the evidence suggests, do not create new wealth. Instead, they help families spread the money they already have across time.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would best support the passage's idea of how microloans help?
choices: Families with microloans started far more new businesses than similar families without loans.
After repaying, borrowers trusted banks more and more often opened savings accounts.
Areas with many lenders had less poverty ten years later than areas with few.
Borrowers earned no more than others but could better pay big, one-time costs.
correct_answer: Borrowers earned no more than others but could better pay big, one-time costs.
key_logic: The passage says borrowers "did not earn more" but could "pay for big, one-time costs," and the key finding matches both halves: no income gain, better handling of large irregular costs.

distractor_map.adapted: Families with microloans started far more new businesses than similar families without loans.
distractor_map.source: Households that received microloans started markedly more new businesses than otherwise similar households that received no loans.
distractor_map.role: supports the business-engine view the passage sets aside

distractor_map.adapted: After repaying, borrowers trusted banks more and more often opened savings accounts.
distractor_map.source: Microloan borrowers reported greater trust in formal financial institutions after repayment, and were likelier than non-borrowers to open a savings account.
distractor_map.role: plausible benefit unrelated to the timing of spending

distractor_map.adapted: Areas with many lenders had less poverty ten years later than areas with few.
distractor_map.source: Regions served by many microfinance institutions had lower overall poverty rates a decade later than otherwise similar regions where such lenders stayed scarce.
distractor_map.role: area-level wealth creation, not household smoothing over time

changes: passage cut from 118 to about 105 words
'randomized trials'/'rigorous evaluations' simplified to 'careful studies'
'smoothing consumption across lean and flush periods' turned into 'get through lean months'
'lumpy purchases' reworded as 'big, one-time costs' in passage and key
stem reworded from 'most strengthen the passage's characterization of microcredit's benefit' to 'best support the passage's idea of how microloans help'
all four findings simplified; none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Many people see farming as an obvious upgrade. Farming made more food, so foragers gladly took it up. Ancient bones tell a different story. Early farmers were shorter than the foragers who came before them. They also had more tooth decay and more signs of poor nutrition. Farming did produce more calories per acre. But those calories came from a few starchy crops, and they cost longer hours of work. Crowded villages also spread disease. So why farm at all? Perhaps once populations had grown, foraging could no longer feed everyone. Farming may have been less a prize than a trap: good for the group's numbers, but bad for each person's health.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's view of the shift to farming?
choices: Some forager groups next to farming villages refused to farm for many centuries.
The first farming villages were bigger and more crowded than earlier forager camps.
Skeletons show the first farmers were taller and better fed than nearby foragers.
Early crops gave many times more calories per acre than wild foods did.
correct_answer: Skeletons show the first farmers were taller and better fed than nearby foragers.
key_logic: The author's evidence that farming hurt individuals is that early farmers "were shorter" and had "more signs of poor nutrition"; skeletons showing farmers taller and better fed would reverse that evidence.

distractor_map.adapted: Some forager groups next to farming villages refused to farm for many centuries.
distractor_map.source: Some forager groups living beside farming villages declined to take up agriculture for many centuries.
distractor_map.role: bears on how fast farming spread, not on farmers' health

distractor_map.adapted: The first farming villages were bigger and more crowded than earlier forager camps.
distractor_map.source: The earliest farming settlements were far larger and more densely settled than the forager camps that preceded them on the same land.
distractor_map.role: fits the argument, since crowding is a named cost

distractor_map.adapted: Early crops gave many times more calories per acre than wild foods did.
distractor_map.source: Early crops delivered several times more calories per acre than the wild foods gathered from the same land.
distractor_map.role: tempting trap: the passage already concedes more calories per acre

changes: passage cut from 144 to about 115 words
'nutritional stress' simplified to 'signs of poor nutrition'; key's 'fewer stress markers' rendered as 'better fed'
'denser settlement that bred infection' turned into 'Crowded villages also spread disease'
stem reworded from 'characterization of the shift to agriculture' to 'view of the shift to farming'
all four findings simplified; none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Many people say that children who speak two languages are better at focusing. They are also said to switch between tasks more easily. The idea is that juggling two languages trains the brain. Early studies seemed to agree. But one scientist doubts it. She points out that many of those studies were small. She also notes that a study was more likely to be published when it found an advantage. She thinks this publishing pattern made the advantage look bigger than it really is. If she is right, she says, the research should show a telltale pattern.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the scientist's idea?
choices: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.
Bilingual adults do better on some focus tasks but not others, mostly ones that need fast switching.
Children who start a second language earlier show bigger advantages than later starters.
Children who speak one language can improve their focus with weeks of special training.
correct_answer: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.
key_logic: The scientist blames a filter that published "small" studies that "found an advantage," so an advantage that shows up only in small studies and disappears in large planned ones is the pattern she predicts.

distractor_map.adapted: Bilingual adults do better on some focus tasks but not others, mostly ones that need fast switching.
distractor_map.source: Bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others, with the gap appearing mainly on tasks that demand rapid switching.
distractor_map.role: a patterned real effect, not a publishing artifact

distractor_map.adapted: Children who start a second language earlier show bigger advantages than later starters.
distractor_map.source: Children who begin a second language earlier show larger executive-function advantages than those who begin later, a dose-response pattern across ages.
distractor_map.role: dose-response pattern pointing to a genuine difference, against her

distractor_map.adapted: Children who speak one language can improve their focus with weeks of special training.
distractor_map.source: Monolingual children can improve their executive function through several weeks of targeted attention training.
distractor_map.role: about training one-language children, a different question

changes: passage cut from 83 to about 95 words (sentences split for grade 7)
'executive-function advantage' simplified to 'better at focusing ... switch between tasks more easily'
'publication filter' explained as 'more likely to be published when it found an advantage'
'pre-registered' rendered as 'planned'
'dose-response pattern across ages' shortened to 'earlier ... than later starters'
stem: 'skeptic's hypothesis' to 'scientist's idea'
none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park. The park then became a famous example of a chain reaction in nature. With wolves back, elk stayed away from open stream banks where they could be ambushed. With less elk grazing, willow and aspen trees grew back along the streams. Newer fieldwork suggests the story is not so simple. Willows have recovered unevenly. They came back strongly where beaver dams raise the water and keep the banks wet. They did poorly where the banks stayed dry, even where wolves were clearly present and elk were clearly cautious. Wolves may be needed for the recovery, but they are not enough on their own.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most support the newer claim that the wolves' return was not enough by itself to bring the trees back?
choices: Elk numbers dropped sharply in the years right after wolves were brought back.
Beaver colonies grew across much of the park after wolves were brought back.
Wolves caught elk most often in open valleys, where herds had few escape routes.
Willows failed where water was low, despite many wolves living there for years.
correct_answer: Willows failed where water was low, despite many wolves living there for years.
key_logic: The newer work says willows "did poorly where the banks stayed dry, even where wolves were clearly present," so willows failing at low water despite years of heavy wolf presence shows wolves alone are not enough.

distractor_map.adapted: Elk numbers dropped sharply in the years right after wolves were brought back.
distractor_map.source: Elk populations fell sharply in the years immediately after wolves were reintroduced.
distractor_map.role: tempting: supports the classic chain reaction, not the qualification

distractor_map.adapted: Beaver colonies grew across much of the park after wolves were brought back.
distractor_map.source: Beaver colonies increased across much of the park following the reintroduction of wolves.
distractor_map.role: fits either story, so distinguishes neither

distractor_map.adapted: Wolves caught elk most often in open valleys, where herds had few escape routes.
distractor_map.source: Wolves hunted elk most successfully in the open bottoms of river valleys, where the browsing herds had few routes of escape.
distractor_map.role: hunting behavior, silent on whether wolves suffice

changes: passage cut from 126 to about 112 words
'trophic cascade' simplified to 'chain reaction in nature'
'raise the water table' simplified to 'raise the water'; 'where those conditions are lacking' made concrete as 'where the banks stayed dry'
'necessary ... not a sufficient one' rendered as 'may be needed ... not enough on their own'
'heavy and sustained wolf presence' rendered as 'many wolves lived there for years'
none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Many people believe that time together makes rival groups less prejudiced. Decades of studies show that contact often does reduce bias. But the idea is not that simple. Early researchers said contact helps only under certain conditions. The groups must meet as equals. They must work toward shared goals, with support from leaders. Without these, contact can make hostility worse. Later studies also found that some of the benefit fades once people leave the planned setting. So the evidence supports a narrower claim. Carefully planned contact reduces prejudice. Simply being around another group will not do the job by itself.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's main claim?
choices: Groups meeting as equals, with shared goals and their leaders' support, became far less biased.
Drops in prejudice from contact faded soon after people left the planned setting.
People who just lived near another group, with no goals or support, grew lastingly less biased.
Contact between unequal, competing groups made the two groups more hostile to each other.
correct_answer: People who just lived near another group, with no goals or support, grew lastingly less biased.
key_logic: The main claim is that "simply being around another group will not do the job by itself," so lasting prejudice reduction from merely living nearby, without the conditions, directly contradicts it.

distractor_map.adapted: Groups meeting as equals, with shared goals and their leaders' support, became far less biased.
distractor_map.source: Evidence that a program meeting the classic conditions—equal status, shared goals, institutional support—sharply reduced participants' bias
distractor_map.role: supports the passage: planned contact works

distractor_map.adapted: Drops in prejudice from contact faded soon after people left the planned setting.
distractor_map.source: A finding that reductions in prejudice from contact tend to fade once participants leave the structured setting
distractor_map.role: matches the passage's own fading-effect qualification

distractor_map.adapted: Contact between unequal, competing groups made the two groups more hostile to each other.
distractor_map.source: A study showing that contact under unequal, competitive conditions increased hostility between groups
distractor_map.role: supports the passage: contact without the conditions backfires

changes: passage cut from 147 to about 105 words
'as anyone who has watched rival factions share cramped quarters can attest' cut
sentence about effects spreading to members never encountered cut (supported no option)
'institutional support' simplified to 'support from leaders'
options turned from noun phrases ('A study showing...') into plain sentences
none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: In the famous "marshmallow test," young children could eat one treat now or wait for two treats later. Those who waited did better later in life. Many took this as proof that self-control is a fixed trait. Some researchers now question that lesson. Waiting only makes sense if a promise can be trusted. A child who has learned that adults often break promises is being sensible by taking the sure treat. When experimenters first showed they were reliable, children waited much longer. When they proved unreliable, even "patient" children grabbed the treat at once. The test may measure not willpower but whether a child expects promises to be kept. That depends on how stable the child's home has been.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most support the researchers' new view of the test?
choices: Longer waiters were more responsible years later, even counting how stable their homes were.
Older children waited longer than younger ones, and the gap grew with each year.
Children from homes often short on food waited less, despite equal self-control test scores.
Children waited just as long after seeing a promise broken as after seeing one kept.
correct_answer: Children from homes often short on food waited less, despite equal self-control test scores.
key_logic: The new view says waiting reflects "whether a child expects promises to be kept" and that this "depends on how stable the child's home has been"; children from unstable homes waiting less while scoring equally on self-control isolates home stability from willpower.

distractor_map.adapted: Longer waiters were more responsible years later, even counting how stable their homes were.
distractor_map.source: Children who waited longer for the treat scored higher on personality measures of conscientiousness years later, and the association held even after researchers adjusted for how stable the child's household had been.
distractor_map.role: supports the fixed-trait reading the passage questions

distractor_map.adapted: Older children waited longer than younger ones, and the gap grew with each year.
distractor_map.source: Older children, on average, waited longer for the delayed reward than younger children did, and the difference widened with each additional year of age.
distractor_map.role: maturation; does not separate trait from expectation

distractor_map.adapted: Children waited just as long after seeing a promise broken as after seeing one kept.
distractor_map.source: Children who had just watched the experimenter break a promise waited as long for the second treat as children who had watched her keep one, whatever the stability of the household they came from.
distractor_map.role: says promise reliability makes no difference, which weakens the view

changes: passage cut from 137 to about 120 words
'evidence-based expectation about whether the world keeps its promises' simplified to 'whether a child expects promises to be kept'
'unpredictable access to food' rendered as 'homes often short on food'
'conscientiousness' simplified to 'being responsible'
stem: 'reconsideration described in the text' to 'researchers' new view of the test'
none dropped (source had four)

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Scientists once marked a small fish called a cleaner wrasse with a colored spot. After the fish saw itself in a mirror, it scraped its body against rocks. Some scientists said this proved the fish was self-aware, like apes and dolphins. We should be careful, though. Passing this mirror test may only show that an animal can link a reflection to its own body. That does not require any idea of a self. The wrasse's way of life gives a simpler answer. This fish gets its food by finding spots on other fish and picking them off. So it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one, even in a mirror.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's simpler reason for what the fish does?
choices: Wrasses try to remove spots on their own bodies even when the spots look like nothing on other fish.
Wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small spots on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Wrasses spend more time looking into a mirror than other reef fish kept in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot much more steadily than wrasses do in the same mirror test.
correct_answer: Wrasses try to remove spots on their own bodies even when the spots look like nothing on other fish.
key_logic: The author explains the scraping by the fish's job of finding spots on other fish ("it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one"), so scraping at spots unlike anything on other fish cannot come from that habit.

distractor_map.adapted: Wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small spots on the bodies of the fish they clean.
distractor_map.source: Cleaner wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small blemishes on the bodies of the fish they clean.
distractor_map.role: supports the author's cleaning-habit explanation instead of weakening it

distractor_map.adapted: Wrasses spend more time looking into a mirror than other reef fish kept in the same tank do.
distractor_map.source: Cleaner wrasses spend more time in front of a mirror than other reef fish placed in the same tank do.
distractor_map.role: shows interest or curiosity, which says nothing about whether a sense of self is involved

distractor_map.adapted: Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot much more steadily than wrasses do in the same mirror test.
distractor_map.source: Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot far more consistently than cleaner wrasses do when the same mark test is administered to both.
distractor_map.role: a difference of degree between species that leaves the author's explanation for the wrasse untouched

changes: passage cut from 144 to 115 words
'sensorimotor achievement that need not involve any concept of a self' turned into 'link a reflection to its own body. That does not require any idea of a self'
'blemish' replaced by 'spot' throughout passage and options
closing sentence about 'the most demanding mechanism' cut (supported no kept option)
stem reworded from 'alternative explanation of the wrasse's behavior' to 'simpler reason for what the fish does'
'mirror' added to the apes-and-dolphins option so it is not unique to the mirror-time option
REPAIR: distractor 'much more often' changed to 'much more steadily' (closer to source 'far more consistently'; now 101 chars vs key 100) so the key is no longer uniquely longest

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: The printing press is often praised for teaching Europe to read, as if cheaper books alone made people readers. The timeline does not support that story. For more than a hundred years, printers mostly served people who could already read, such as priests, lawyers, and merchants. Most early books were church texts and scholarly works in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. In many regions, reading rates barely changed until much later, when church campaigns and school programs gave ordinary people a reason to read and lessons in how to do it. Printing made those later efforts cheaper. On its own, though, it supplied neither the reason nor the teaching.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
choices: Where printing came early, reading rates rose sharply only many years later, once church schools opened.
Across Europe, the number of books grew many times over within a few short decades of the first printing.
Early printers fought hard with one another to sell Latin copies of old Greek and Roman books.
Reading rates rose fastest in the first years after printing began, well before any schools opened.
correct_answer: Where printing came early, reading rates rose sharply only many years later, once church schools opened.
key_logic: The author says reading rates "barely changed until much later, when church campaigns and school programs" arrived, so a sharp rise only many years later, after church schools opened, matches that timeline.

distractor_map.adapted: Across Europe, the number of books grew many times over within a few short decades of the first printing.
distractor_map.source: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
distractor_map.role: measures how many books were printed, which the author separates from how many people could read

distractor_map.adapted: Early printers fought hard with one another to sell Latin copies of old Greek and Roman books.
distractor_map.source: Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
distractor_map.role: fits the passage but says nothing about when or why reading rates rose

distractor_map.adapted: Reading rates rose fastest in the first years after printing began, well before any schools opened.
distractor_map.source: Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.
distractor_map.role: contradicts the argument by crediting printing alone

'confessional campaigns and schooling drives' simplified to 'church campaigns and school programs'
final 'necessary instrument ... not the cause' sentence folded into 'On its own, though, it supplied neither the reason nor the teaching'
'learned tomes' replaced by 'scholarly works'; 'clergy, jurists' by 'priests, lawyers'
option 'Latin editions of the classical authors' simplified to 'Latin copies of old Greek and Roman books'; key 'generations later' simplified to 'many years later'
'literacy' replaced by 'reading rates' in passage and options
REPAIR: distractor 'within a few decades' changed to 'within a few short decades' (now 105 chars vs key 104) so the key is no longer uniquely longest

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: When photos showed narrow gullies on the walls of craters on Mars, many people thought flowing water had carved them. If so, Mars might once have been friendly to life. The gullies do look like channels that water cuts on Earth. But looking alike does not prove the same cause. Many of the gullies sit in places too cold for liquid water to last. They are also most active in the middle of winter, not in summer. That is when frozen carbon dioxide, called dry ice, builds up and then turns straight into gas. So many scientists now think the gullies were carved by blocks of dry ice sliding on the gas they give off.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most support the dry-ice explanation over the water explanation?
choices: Photos show gully rock moving in the coldest months, when dry ice forms and any water would be frozen solid.
The gullies on Mars look very much like the channels that rain runoff cuts into desert slopes on Earth.
Clay that forms only after long contact with liquid water was found in old rock far from the gullies.
The gullies lie on slopes steep enough for loose rock to slide down by gravity alone, with no water or dry ice.
correct_answer: Photos show gully rock moving in the coldest months, when dry ice forms and any water would be frozen solid.
key_logic: The passage says the gullies are "most active in the middle of winter" when dry ice builds up and it is "too cold for liquid water," so movement in the coldest months fits dry ice and rules out water.

distractor_map.adapted: The gullies on Mars look very much like the channels that rain runoff cuts into desert slopes on Earth.
distractor_map.source: The Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth.
distractor_map.role: resemblance that leans toward water, which the passage says does not prove the cause

distractor_map.adapted: Clay that forms only after long contact with liquid water was found in old rock far from the gullies.
distractor_map.source: Clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water have been identified in ancient terrain far from the gullies.
distractor_map.role: evidence about water on ancient Mars elsewhere, not about what carved these gullies

distractor_map.adapted: The gullies lie on slopes steep enough for loose rock to slide down by gravity alone, with no water or dry ice.
distractor_map.source: The gullies sit on slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone, without any lubricant.
distractor_map.role: fits either cause equally, so it cannot separate the two explanations

changes: passage kept near length (116 to 115 words) with sentences shortened (definition of dry ice added: 'frozen carbon dioxide, called dry ice')
'sublimates' turned into 'turns straight into gas'
'lubricated by the gas they release' turned into 'sliding on the gas they give off'
closing sentence 'the gullies say little about Mars's habitability' cut (supported no option)
stem reworded from 'carbon-dioxide hypothesis over the water hypothesis' to 'dry-ice explanation over the water explanation'

key 'CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist' simplified to 'dry ice forms and any water would be frozen solid'; 'time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving' to 'photos show gully rock moving'
gravity option 'without any lubricant' reworded to 'with no water or dry ice' so 'dry ice' is not unique to the key

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: It sounds strange that a warming planet could make part of Europe colder, but the ocean explains how. A huge Atlantic current carries warm water from the tropics north toward Europe. The current is driven partly by cold, salty water sinking in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it pours fresh water into that area. Fresh water is lighter, so it does not sink as easily. The current then slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. Scientists are careful about this claim. They do not predict a new ice age, and they agree that the planet as a whole keeps warming. They say only that a warmer world could still produce a cooler northwestern Europe.
prompt: Which observation would most support the process described in the passage?
choices: As more fresh water flowed into the North Atlantic, deep water sank more slowly and less heat moved north.
Across all of Europe, it got colder even as the world as a whole got warmer.
Greenland's ice sheet lost ice faster in warmer years, and more of it melted off its edges during each hot summer.
Ocean water in the tropics warmed at the same pace as the world as a whole did.
correct_answer: As more fresh water flowed into the North Atlantic, deep water sank more slowly and less heat moved north.
key_logic: The passage's chain is that fresh water "does not sink as easily," so "the current then slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe"; the observation shows each link happening.

distractor_map.adapted: Across all of Europe, it got colder even as the world as a whole got warmer.
distractor_map.source: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
distractor_map.role: overstates the hedged claim, which is limited to northwestern Europe

distractor_map.adapted: Greenland's ice sheet lost ice faster in warmer years, and more of it melted off its edges during each hot summer.
distractor_map.source: Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years, shedding meltwater from its margins at rates that tracked each summer's temperatures.
distractor_map.role: confirms the melting that starts the chain but says nothing about the current

distractor_map.adapted: Ocean water in the tropics warmed at the same pace as the world as a whole did.
distractor_map.source: Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.
distractor_map.role: concerns where the heat comes from, not whether the current still carries it north

'conveyor' replaced by 'huge Atlantic current'; 'less dense' by 'lighter'
'a global mean temperature can conceal opposing regional trends' cut; 'nor that regional cooling would offset global warming' turned into 'they agree that the planet as a whole keeps warming'
stem 'mechanism described in the text' reworded to 'process described in the passage'
key 'northward transport of heat weakened' simplified to 'less heat moved north'

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Most histories say Japan built factories quickly after 1868 for one reason. Its new Meiji government brought in Western machines and foreign advisers. The machines mattered, but they do not explain why Japan could put them to use when many other countries could not. Long before 1868, Japan already had high literacy, busy trade networks, and skilled village workshops. Its merchant houses kept careful account books. So the new machines met workers and managers who were ready to run them. Foreign experts were sent home as soon as Japanese workers could replace them, often within ten years. Japan's success came less from borrowing than from business skills it already had.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's main claim?
choices: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machines than any other country in Asia did then.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid much more than they had earned at home, a bonus that drew many engineers.
Before 1868, reading rates in Japan's country villages were much lower than in its large cities.
correct_answer: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.
key_logic: The author credits skills "it already had" rather than the machines, so a country with the same machines but without those skills falling behind isolates the skills as the cause.

distractor_map.adapted: The Meiji government spent more on foreign machines than any other country in Asia did then.
distractor_map.source: The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
distractor_map.role: measures the borrowing the author plays down, not Japan's own skills

distractor_map.adapted: Foreign advisers in Japan were paid much more than they had earned at home, a bonus that drew many engineers.
distractor_map.source: Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home, a premium that drew engineers and accountants to Meiji ministries.
distractor_map.role: true-sounding detail about cost that has no bearing on the claim

distractor_map.adapted: Before 1868, reading rates in Japan's country villages were much lower than in its large cities.
distractor_map.source: Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.
distractor_map.role: chips at the skilled village base the author relies on, weakening rather than strengthening

'rural proto-industry' simplified to 'skilled village workshops'; 'double-entry accounting and futures trading' to 'kept careful account books'

'redirecting indigenous capacities toward national ends' and final 'visible surface of a deeper continuity' sentence cut, replaced by 'Japan's success came less from borrowing than from business skills it already had'
'Commodore Perry' / 'Tokugawa' replaced by 'Long before 1868' and 'Before 1868'
stem 'central claim' reworded to 'main claim'
key 'comparable commercial institutions' simplified to 'those business skills'; 'failed to industrialize at a similar pace' to 'built factories more slowly'

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: The "hygiene hypothesis" is often told as a simple warning. Modern homes are so clean that children meet few germs. As a result, their immune systems never learn properly, and allergies follow. Most immune scientists no longer accept that version. The rise in allergies does not match up well with fewer common childhood illnesses, such as colds and flu. Instead, it matches up with less contact with certain ancient, mostly harmless microbes. These "old friends" evolved alongside humans and help tune the immune system. In this newer view, a childhood full of colds gives little protection, while contact with the right microbes from the environment does.
prompt: Which finding would best support the newer view rather than the popular version?
choices: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.
Children raised in very clean homes with almost no germs had far more allergies than children from less clean homes.
Adults who often catch colds and flu tend to have weaker immune systems than adults who rarely get sick.
The "old friend" microbes were far more common in human homes thousands of years ago than in homes today.
correct_answer: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.
key_logic: The newer view says "a childhood full of colds gives little protection, while contact with the right microbes from the environment does," and the finding shows both halves.

distractor_map.role: fits the popular slogan just as well, so it does not separate the two versions

distractor_map.source: The 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago than they are in the households of modern industrialized countries today.
distractor_map.role: consistent with the newer view but gives no evidence about who develops allergies
